44.0.0.en: 1- “We have heard with our ears, O God, our fathers have told us, what work thou didst in their days, in the times of old.”

44.0.1.en: 1- The writer of the psalm declares about himself and the congregation of believers with him that they heard assured words, for he said we have heard with our ears words about God in the ages before them, by way of the fathers and the prophets, who had a strong connection with God. And the reports were handed down from fathers to sons.

44.0.2.en: 2- When he says “we have heard with our ears” this signifies the Incarnation, for he tells us about the tangible God in the Old Testament by way of the fathers and prophets, who appeared plainly in the fullness of time by His Incarnation.

44.1.0.en: 2- “Thou hast uprooted the nations with thy hand, and planted them; thou hast shattered peoples and spread them out.”

44.1.1.en: Spread them out: gave them expansion and breadth and dominion over many lands.

44.1.2.en: 1- The work of God appears in shattering and uprooting the pagan nations that dwelt in the land of Canaan, who were strong peoples; because they worshiped idols and were immersed in evil lusts. And on the other side He planted and established His children, and gave them possession of this fertile land flowing with milk and honey, and extended their hands to take dominion over lands that were not theirs. For God removes evil and establishes good, that is, His children who believe in Him and live by His commandments.

44.1.3.en: 2- The Incarnation of Christ also appears in this verse by his saying “with thy hand.” And by this He removed our mortal evil nature, which is signified by the nations that He uprooted and shattered. And He gave us the new nature inclined to good, which is signified by His children whom He planted and spread out in the land of Canaan.

44.2.0.en: 3- “For they got not the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them: but thy right hand, and thine arm, and the light of thy countenance, because thou hadst a favour unto them.”

44.2.1.en: 1- Here he confirms that the power of victory which was with the people of God, which made them overcome their enemies, drive them out, and possess their land, was not due to their weapons or their human strength, but its source was God, who struck Egypt with the ten plagues, split the Red Sea, drowned Pharaoh and his army, stopped the sun for Joshua, and brought down the walls of Jericho ... because God was pleased with His people and loved them, since they believed in Him and kept His commandments. This is the communal salvation that God gave to His people.

44.2.2.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about the incarnate Christ, who is signified by His right hand and His arm and the light of His countenance, for He is the source of the strength of those who believe in Him, and defeats their enemies the demons, and even gives them possession of the places of the demons who fell, so that they reign with Him in heaven.

44.2.3.en: 3- This verse also applies to the Apostles and their preaching, for they did not uproot idolatry and shatter it by a sword or human strength, but by the word of God and His power.

44.3.0.en: 4- “Thou art my King, O God: command deliverances for Jacob.”

44.3.1.en: The writer of the psalm feels God's strength supporting him, so he submits to Him, and God reigns over his heart, until he calls Him with boldness, O my King. And with this boldness he asks Him for salvation for all his people. This salvation is accomplished by God's command, that is, by a mere word from Him, so he is rid of his enemies and defeats them.

44.4.0.en: 5- “Through thee we push down our oppressors: through thy name we tread down those who rise up against us.”

44.4.1.en: As the writer of the psalm felt God's strength and salvation, he was encouraged to storm the enemies and the opponents, and to gore them like a horned animal and destroy them, and the horns signify strength, and after he throws them on the ground he tramples them and crushes them. And this is what the children of God believe in the New Testament, that they have authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy. So the believer feels the power of God within him, and does not fear sin, or Satan, or the wicked, but attacks them by the power of God, and triumphs over them.

44.5.0.en: 6- “For I do not trust in my bow, neither shall my sword save me. 7- But thou hast saved us from our oppressors, and hast put to shame those who hate us.”

44.5.1.en: The writer of the psalm declares that he will do his duty in the war, and arm himself with the bow and the sword, which are the weapons known in war at that time. But his reliance is on the power of God which gives him victory, and not on weapons. And as God saved the fathers of old from their enemies (v. 3) He will save His people, for the writer relies on God, and trusts that He will save all his people and give them victory.

44.6.0.en: 8- “In God we boast all the day long, and praise thy name for ever. Selah.”

44.6.1.en: 1- The writer believed in the power of God which has worked, and will continue to work with him and with his people. For this reason he raised his voice in thanksgiving, praise, and boasting in the work of God all the day long, that is, all his life, and even forever, and this confirms his faith in the eternal life that God has prepared for him. And the writer boasts in the work of God, whether periods of rest or affliction pass over him; because he trusts that after the affliction he will obtain God's victory in him, for the day includes the daytime and the night, that is, rest and affliction.

44.6.2.en: 2- This verse is the voice of all the believers in the New Testament, who give thanks to God through the Sacrament of Thanksgiving, that is, partaking of the Holy Mysteries, and enjoy His constant work in them, and their victory over the demons, until He brings them to the Kingdom.

44.6.3.en: 3- At the end of this verse there is the word “Selah,” which is a musical pause for meditation on the power of God that supports His children, and that we may lift up our hearts with thanksgiving and praise to Him.

44.6.4.en: Rely on God at all times, confident of His power and His support which gives you victory in all your spiritual wars, and thank Him always for His past works, so that His work in your life extends forever.

44.7.0.en: 9- “But thou hast rejected us, and put us to shame; and goest not forth with our armies.”

44.7.1.en: After God supported His people and gave them victory over their enemies, He returned and forsook them, and rejected them; why?

44.7.2.en: 1- So that they may discover their sins and repent of them, and God returns and gives them victory.

44.7.3.en: 2- So that they may be sure that their strength is from God, and not from their weapons or their personal strength.

44.7.4.en: 3- So that their faith and steadfastness in God may be tested despite defeat and shame.

44.7.5.en: And this happened after Joshua's victory over the inhabitants of Canaan; they returned and were defeated before them in the days of the Judges (Judg 2:21-23). And as the Jews triumphed in the days of David and Solomon, they returned and were defeated and were taken captive to Assyria, then Babylon. And as they triumphed in the days of the Maccabees, but they returned and were defeated before the Greeks, and after their repentance they regained their victory.

44.8.0.en: 10- “Thou makest us turn back from the enemy, and those who hate us plunder for themselves. 11- Thou hast made us like sheep to be eaten; thou hast scattered us among the nations.”

44.8.1.en: Thou hast scattered us: dispersed us.

44.8.2.en: When God forsook His people the enemies triumphed over them, so the people turned back defeated, and the enemy even seized the spoils that were with the people of God, and took from them slaves for himself, and slaughtered many of the people of God, as sheep are slaughtered, and the rest of the people of God the enemy scattered everywhere on the earth. This is what happened in the days of the Assyrian captivity, then the Babylonian, and as happened with the Christians in the Jewish persecution in the days of the Apostles, when they killed many of them, and the rest were scattered in the various countries of the world. And this divine forsaking may be because of the pride of the people of God, so God allows them weakness before their enemies, that they may be humbled, and repent and pray, and He returns and rescues them and glorifies them.

44.9.0.en: 12- “Thou sellest thy people for nought, and dost not increase thy wealth by their price.”

44.9.1.en: The writer reproaches God, who forsook His people, so He sold them to their enemies, without profiting anything from selling them; because the cause was the sin of His people, that they might repent. Although it is a reproach of God, it is at the same time the writer's reproach of his people, to let them know that the cause of their discipline is their sin, so that they repent; and if it is not because of sin, they obtain approval, strength and grace from God.

44.10.0.en: 13- “Thou makest us a reproach to our neighbours, a scorn and a derision to them that are round about us. 14- Thou makest us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples.”

44.10.1.en: A shaking of the head: shaking the head in mockery and contempt of another.

44.10.2.en: God did not only forsake His people and leave them to be defeated before their enemies, but He also humbled them among their neighbors, who saw their former glory, and now see them fleeing and their cities ruined. And God allowed this humiliation so that the people might be humbled and return to God. This reproach of God shows the writer's faith, his holding fast to prayer, and therefore his readiness for repentance, or it is, in other words, calling his people to repentance, after their neighbors from the nations mocked them and despised them. And these neighbors are the peoples of Palestine, Edom, Moab, and the sons of Ammon, and the Edomites would even seize the Jews who fled and deliver them to the Babylonians (Obad 1:10-14).

44.11.0.en: 15- “All the day my confusion is before me, and the shame of my face hath covered me, 16- From the voice of him that reproacheth and gloats, from the face of the enemy and avenger.”

44.11.1.en: 1- The people of God were affected by their enemies' contempt of them and their vengeance on them, and the people were in shame and disgrace for a long period, which is the period of the captivity that lasted seventy years. But this divine humbling led to repentance, so they enjoyed returning from captivity and building the temple.

44.11.2.en: 2- These two verses and what precedes them apply to Christ (vv. 13-16), who bore our sins and suffered for us, and bore the cross of shame and disgrace to redeem us. And by His death for us He saved us, then rose in glory to raise us up in Him.

44.11.3.en: 3- These verses apply to the Christians whom the pagans around them reproached, for their worship of the person of the Crucified, weak, in shame and disgrace, but God glorified them with many miracles while they bore the torments, then gave them crowns of glory in heaven.

44.11.4.en: Accept God's discipline, for it is profitable for your salvation, to purify you from your sins and approve you, so that you obtain great blessings and are made worthy of the Kingdom of Heaven.

44.12.0.en: 17- “All this is come upon us; yet have we not forgotten thee, neither have we dealt falsely in thy covenant. 18- Our heart is not turned back, neither have our steps declined from thy way.”

44.12.1.en: 1- Despite the divine disciplines that the verses mentioned from (vv. 9-16) the children of God remained holding fast to their faith and their covenants with Him, as happened in the days of the Maccabees when the Greeks persecuted them and tried to force them to worship idols, and wronged them, but they held fast to their faith (1 Macc 1:65, 66), and as the saints stood firm despite the afflictions surrounding them in captivity, such as Tobit and Daniel and the three youths...

44.12.2.en: 2- These verses are a prophecy about the Christians who bore persecutions, and stood firm in the faith, and bore torments to the point of martyrdom in the days of the Jewish persecution, or the Roman, or any later persecutions.

44.13.0.en: 19- “Though thou hast sore broken us in the place of dragons, and covered us with the shadow of death.”

44.13.1.en: Dragons: plural of dragon, a strong and very predatory animal. It was known in ancient times, and does not exist now, and it is used to refer to any predatory animal.

44.13.2.en: The place of dragons is the hardest place in which human beings can be found; because they are exposed to being crushed by these dragons in their ferocity and violence. This is what the writer of the psalm wants to express by the extent of the distress into which the people of God entered, and he also expressed this distress as the shadow of death that covered the people of God, and despite the severity of the afflictions they did not leave God.

44.14.0.en: 20- “If we have forgotten the name of our God, or stretched out our hands to a strange god; 21- Shall not God search this out? for he knoweth the secrets of the heart.”

44.14.1.en: The writer confirms the purity of his heart, and declares that he and his people could not have betrayed God, or forgotten Him and neglected Him, or lifted their hands in prayer to another god; because God searches everything, and knows all secrets. He does not only know that they worship God, but knows that their hearts love Him, and they hold fast to their faith. So the writer has no need to show God that his people believe in Him; because God knows everything.

44.15.0.en: 22- “Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.”

44.15.1.en: 1- The love of the people of God and their steadfastness in faith appear in their readiness to die all the day long, and by the day is meant all the days of life, that is, their constant readiness to bear all pains even to death. And in this they are like sheep led to be slaughtered, which are ready for the slaughter at any time. And this is a love above which no other love can rise, and this is what Christ accomplished on the Cross.

44.15.2.en: 2- Every person who strives spiritually against sin gives up and strips himself of many things, and humbles himself. These are kinds of death for the sake of God, and likewise everyone who serves God laying down his life for him to bring His children back to Him, for service is a kind of death. In sum, the spiritual man who strives is ready to die for the sake of God all his life. And this is martyrdom, for the martyrs are not only those who were tortured and slaughtered for the sake of God, but everyone who strives in his spiritual life, and toils in service, as the Apostle Paul said (Rom 8:36).

44.15.3.en: Be steadfast in your faith, and keep God's commandments however differently the people around you behave and think of you. And bear their doubts, provocations and opposition to you, for your steadfastness is of very great value before God.

44.16.s.en: (4) A cry for help and self-abasement

44.16.0.en: 23- “Awake, why dost thou slumber, O Lord? Attend, cast us not off for ever. 24- Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and forgettest our affliction and our oppression?”

44.16.1.en: Dost thou slumber: be not in a doze, that is, do not sleep, and leave us in our distress.

44.16.2.en: 1- The writer of the psalm expresses his suffering in the affliction with all his people, and calls on God to hasten to their aid; because God in His silence and long-suffering seems as though He were asleep and inattentive, or rejecting His people, or hiding His face from them, or neglecting and forgetting their toils. All this shows the severity of the people's suffering and its great need for God's intervention to rescue it, for it is a kind of reproach, with the boldness of sonship, from the people to God.

44.16.3.en: 2- These two verses resemble the words of the disciples in their reproach of Christ asleep in the hold of the ship, while the winds almost sank the ship (Mt 8:25). Every spiritual person needs to awaken the Christ who sleeps within him, to ward off from him the winds of trials and the wars of the devil, and to rescue him from every sin.

44.17.0.en: 25- “For our soul is bowed down to the dust: our belly cleaveth unto the earth.”

44.17.1.en: The writer expresses the extent of the abasement and humiliation to which the people of God had come, saying that their souls were brought low until they clung to the dust of the earth, and likewise their bellies, that is, they were in a spiritual and psychological abasement because of the afflictions through which they pass. So this verse shows the bitterness of their souls, and their great need for God's help. And their request in humility that God raise them up and lift them.

44.18.0.en: 26- “Arise for our help, and redeem us for thy mercies' sake.” The writer declares clearly that the only solution to rescue the people of God from their abasement is for God to intervene with His help, indeed that God come forward and redeem His people, that is, rescue them from the hands of their enemies, and destroy the wicked. And this verse is a clear prophecy about Christ the Redeemer, who justifies those who believe in Him, and binds Satan.

44.18.1.en: When the affliction increases and weighs heavily on you, trust that God your Redeemer is able to lift it from you; indeed when the affliction grows heavier, it means that its solution has drawn near.

44.18.2.en: Longing for God. To the choirmaster - a poem for the sons of Korah “As the hart longs for the water brooks” (v. 1) Introduction:

44.18.4.en: A - Some see that they are the sons of Korah who did not die with Korah in his murmuring against the priesthood (Num 26:11), especially since some of them were exposed to exile at the River Jordan, as mentioned in (v. 6). And the writer of this psalm was accustomed to lead those going up to the temple in singing (v. 4).

44.18.5.en: B - David is its writer and the sons of Korah are those who set it to music, and this is the more probable opinion, by the evidence that the writer of the psalm speaks in the singular, and mentions the word “my soul” as in (vv. 1, 2). And the places mentioned in (v. 6) were places where David was exiled during King Saul's pursuit of him, and it is thought that David wrote this psalm when Absalom drove him out of his kingdom.

44.18.6.en: 2- This psalm shows man's longings for the temple of God, and for being with God, and his suffering at his distance from the communal worship in the temple, as he feels that God alone is able to quench the thirst of his soul.

44.18.7.en: 3- This psalm is linked to the psalm that follows it in its subject, to the point that some scholars thought the two psalms to be one poem, especially since the first section and the second section in this psalm each end with the same verse, which is also the same verse with which Ps 43 ends (Ps 42:5; Ps 43:5), and therefore it was considered a refrain repeated in this one poem, which is considered a personal lament, expressing the pains of the past, present and future from which the writer suffers.

44.18.8.en: 4- The eight psalms from Ps 42 to Ps 49 are of the composition, or setting to music, of the sons of Korah.

44.18.9.en: 5- This psalm may be a prophecy about the griefs of the captives in Babylon, who long to return to Jerusalem, and it is also a prophecy about the longings of the believers in the Old Testament for the Church of Christ in the New Testament, and represents all the believers who are strangers on earth, and who long for the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven.

44.18.10.en: 6- This psalm is the first psalm of the second section according to the division of the Jews, which begins with this psalm and ends with Psalm 72.

44.18.11.en: 7- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
